title: SE201 Lesson 8: Routines, pipelines, and integration

data.sub: From loop to enterprise systems  •  clarkhuang.github.io

scenes.text: Quick question. It's two in the morning. A job charges a customer's card. The payment goes through, but the connection drops before the answer comes back. So the job tries again. [pause] What happens? Nothing? The customer is charged twice? Or the processor catches it on its own? [pause] <emphasis>Quite possibly, charged twice.</emphasis> Some processors catch a quick duplicate, but don't count on it. Design the retry to be safe. That design is this lesson.

scenes.text: Connecting systems is the oldest problem in this series. Thirty years ago: overnight batch files, and E.D.I. Then web services. Then an A.P.I. for everything. Now, agents calling tools. [pause] And every one of those is still running somewhere, often inside the same enterprise.

data.label: INTEGRATION  ·  THE OLDEST PROBLEM IN THIS SERIES

nodes.text: One enterprise, today: often several of these at once

data.caption: Every one of them is still running somewhere.

scenes.text: A skill is one job, written down and tested, that runs when someone asks. But some work should start on its own. On a schedule: every night at two. On an event: a payment fails, or a file arrives. Or when the step before it finishes. [pause] Call a skill plus a trigger a routine. And routines, chained, make a pipeline.

data.label: WORK THAT STARTS ON ITS OWN  ·  THREE KINDS OF TRIGGER

nodes.sub: A payment fails · a file arrives

data.caption: A skill + a trigger: a routine.  Routines, chained: a pipeline.

scenes.text: Here's one, in our made-up subscription-billing system: the nightly billing run. On a schedule, find the renewals due. Charge each one, through the payment processor. Write the invoices. Send the export to the accounting system. And last, reconcile: does our ledger match what the processor says it charged?

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE NIGHTLY BILLING RUN
data.caption: Five steps, chained. The first starts on a schedule.

scenes.text: Between every two steps, something crosses: the renewals due, the charge results, the invoices, the export file. Give each a clear, written format. Then any step can be rebuilt, or rerun, without touching the others.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE NIGHTLY BILLING RUN
data.caption: A clear, written format at every hand-off.

scenes.text: And every step leaves a record: what came in, what went out, what failed. A thousand renewals due. Nine hundred eighty-eight charged, twelve declined. Nine hundred eighty-eight invoices, and as many rows sent. The numbers are made up, but they have to add up. When they don't, the run stops there, and you know which step to open.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE, MADE-UP NUMBERS  ·  THE NIGHTLY BILLING RUN
data.caption:
Every step leaves a record. The counts have to add up.
When they don’t, the run stops there.

scenes.text: Back to two A.M. Partway through the charge step, the connection drops. One charge went out, and no answer came back. Did it go through? We don't know. [pause] So the retry has to be safe to run twice. Renewals already recorded as charged, it skips. Every other one, it sends with a key that never changes: this subscription, this billing period. If the processor has already seen that key, it returns the first result, instead of charging again. That's an idempotency key, and many payment processors support one.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE NIGHTLY BILLING RUN

fail.title: INSIDE THE CHARGE STEP  ·  EACH BLOCK IS ONE RENEWAL
fail.sub2: Seen the key? Same answer back
fail.key: key = this subscription + this billing period

data.caption: Safe to run twice: skip what’s recorded as charged; send the rest, each with its own key.

scenes.text: Last, reconcile compares our ledger with the processor's record. If they don't match, the pipeline doesn't guess, and doesn't fix the numbers itself. It keeps every record, and tells a person. [pause] Most of these steps are plain code. An agent earns its place where a step needs judgment, like working out why they don't match.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE NIGHTLY BILLING RUN

alert.text:
Doesn’t match?
Don’t guess. Keep every record.
Tell a person.

data.caption:
Most steps: plain code.
An agent: where a step needs judgment.

scenes.text: The same thinking covers everything you don't control. Take a partner's nightly file. Check it first. Late: wait, then alert. Twice: recognize it, and skip it. Broken: set it aside, and tell a person. [pause] You can't count on anything arriving exactly once. So design for at least once, and make twice harmless.

data.label: YOU DEPEND ON THINGS YOU DON’T CONTROL  ·  A PARTNER’S NIGHTLY FILE

nodes.text: Broken: set it aside, tell a person

data.caption: Design for at least once. Make twice harmless.

scenes.text: So, to recap. Give every hand-off a clear format. Make every step leave a record that adds up. Make every step safe to run twice. And when the numbers don't match, stop, and tell a person.

data.headline: Routines, pipelines, integration

Every step leaves a record that adds up
Every step is safe to run twice
Doesn’t match? Stop, and tell a person

scenes.text: Which gives us rule eight, for your agents. Before any work runs on its own, write down four things. What starts it. What crosses at each hand-off. What record each step leaves. And what happens when a step fails, or runs twice. No answer? It isn't ready to run unattended.

lines.text: Before any work runs on its own, write down:
and what happens when a step fails, or runs twice.
No answer? It isn’t ready to run unattended.

data.foot: THE FULL RULE IS ON THE LESSON PAGE

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Pick one job that already runs on its own: a nightly report, or a sync. Describe its steps to your A.I., and ask, for each step: what happens if it runs twice? And what record would prove it ran? [pause] The steps with no good answer are where to start.

data.headline:
Your turn. One job that runs on its own.
Ask your AI, for each step:
what happens if it runs twice?
What record would prove it ran?

scenes.text: A pipeline that runs on its own is already operating the system. So whose name does it run under? What is it allowed to touch? And who can see what it did? [pause] That's next: agents that operate enterprise systems. See you in lesson nine.
